title: CPU Frequency Scaling Events
exclusions: Measures changes in the Linux CPUFreq statistics counter for each kernel policy; it does not observe every hardware P-state change, prove thermal throttling, measure CPU utilization, or diagnose why the governor requested a frequency. `scaling_cur_freq` is retained only as optional context in kHz and is not treated as an event. The use case does not cover systems without `CONFIG_CPU_FREQ_STAT`, firmware-only frequency management, guests exposing no meaningful CPUFreq policy, CPU hot-plug diagnosis, power consumption, or regulatory compliance. Linux Audit file watches and systemd journal messages are deliberately excluded because kernel updates to CPUFreq sysfs attributes are not documented as audit `action=modified` or journal events.
evidence: For an implemented deployment, retain the versioned saved-search definition and dispatch history for `linux_cpufreq_transition_rate_5m`, representative raw `linux:cpufreq:stats` JSON samples before and during the finding, the governed `linux_cpufreq_thresholds.csv` row, effective scripted-input configuration from `splunk btool inputs list --debug`, and the incident, benchmark, or change-ticket disposition. These artefacts demonstrate observed CPUFreq counter deltas and alert execution; they do not prove a thermal or hardware fault.

controlTest.positiveScenario: In a nonproduction `index=os` fixture for host `cpufreq-test-01` and policy `policy0`, index five `linux:cpufreq:stats` JSON samples 60 seconds apart in one completed five-minute bucket with `total_trans` values 1000, 1060, 1120, 1180, and 1240, constant `scaling_driver=acpi-cpufreq`, `scaling_governor=schedutil`, and valid `sample_epoch` values. Add one exact `linux_cpufreq_thresholds.csv` row with `max_transitions_per_minute=30`, `min_observed_seconds=180`, and `threshold_enabled=1`. With no active exception, the saved search must return one row with `transition_count=240`, `observed_seconds=240`, and `transitions_per_minute=60`.
controlTest.negativeScenario: In the same isolated source, index five samples whose `scaling_cur_freq` alternates between 1200000 and 3000000 kHz but whose `total_trans` remains 500; this sampled-frequency movement alone must return zero rows. Also test a counter reset from 500 to 3: the decreasing interval must be discarded rather than interpreted as a large transition count. Finally, set an exact active `linux_cpufreq_exceptions.csv` row for `cpufreq-test-01,policy0`; an otherwise positive sequence must produce zero alert rows while remaining searchable in the raw source.

dataSources: One JSON event per CPUFreq policy per poll, collected into the local convention `index=os sourcetype=linux:cpufreq:stats` by a Universal Forwarder `[script://...]` input. The script reads `/sys/devices/system/cpu/cpufreq/policy*/stats/total_trans` plus optional policy attributes and emits `sample_epoch, policy, total_trans, affected_cpus, related_cpus, scaling_driver, scaling_governor, current_frequency_khz`. The SPL also requires exact-key lookup definitions `linux_cpufreq_thresholds` and `linux_cpufreq_exceptions`. Neither `linux_audit` nor the systemd journal supplies this field contract.
app: Splunk Universal Forwarder built-in scripted-input facility plus a locally maintained `linux_cpufreq` deployment app and host-provided Python 3 runtime; no Splunkbase add-on or premium Splunk app is required. Splunk Add-on for Unix and Linux is not the source of the CPUFreq policy fields used here.
spl:
index=os sourcetype=linux:cpufreq:stats
| spath
| eval sample_epoch=tonumber(sample_epoch), total_trans=tonumber(total_trans), current_frequency_khz=tonumber(current_frequency_khz)
| eval _time=coalesce(sample_epoch,_time)
| where isnotnull(policy) AND isnotnull(total_trans)
| sort 0 host policy _time
| streamstats current=f window=1 last(total_trans) as previous_total_trans last(_time) as previous_time by host policy
| eval observed_seconds=_time-previous_time, transition_delta=if(total_trans>=previous_total_trans,total_trans-previous_total_trans,null())
| where observed_seconds>0 AND isnotnull(transition_delta)
| eval _time=round((_time+previous_time)/2,0)
| bin _time span=5m
| stats sum(transition_delta) as transition_count sum(observed_seconds) as observed_seconds latest(current_frequency_khz) as current_frequency_khz latest(scaling_driver) as scaling_driver latest(scaling_governor) as scaling_governor values(affected_cpus) as affected_cpus by _time host policy
| eval current_frequency_mhz=round(current_frequency_khz/1000,1), transitions_per_minute=round(transition_count*60/observed_seconds,2)
| lookup linux_cpufreq_thresholds host policy OUTPUT max_transitions_per_minute min_observed_seconds threshold_enabled
| eval max_transitions_per_minute=tonumber(max_transitions_per_minute), min_observed_seconds=tonumber(min_observed_seconds), threshold_enabled=tonumber(threshold_enabled)
| where threshold_enabled=1 AND isnotnull(max_transitions_per_minute) AND observed_seconds>=min_observed_seconds AND transitions_per_minute>max_transitions_per_minute
| lookup linux_cpufreq_exceptions host policy OUTPUT exception_start_epoch exception_end_epoch exception_enabled exception_ticket
| eval exception_active=if(coalesce(tonumber(exception_enabled),0)=1 AND now()>=coalesce(tonumber(exception_start_epoch),0) AND now()<=coalesce(tonumber(exception_end_epoch),32503680000),1,0)
| where exception_active=0
| table _time host policy scaling_driver scaling_governor affected_cpus transition_count observed_seconds transitions_per_minute max_transitions_per_minute current_frequency_khz current_frequency_mhz
| sort 0 -_time host policy
description: Calculates five-minute CPU frequency-transition rates from successive Linux CPUFreq `stats/total_trans` samples, separately for each host and kernel policy. A result requires sufficient observation time, an enabled host/policy threshold, a rate above that threshold, and no active exact-key exception. Counter decreases are treated as resets, while `scaling_cur_freq` is shown only as point-in-time context.
value: Unexpected transition churn can reveal a governor, firmware, workload, or power-policy change that warrants performance investigation, especially when it coincides with latency regressions. Policy-specific baselines keep the signal useful across dissimilar drivers and workloads, and the retained driver, governor, CPU set, rate, and raw counters give platform engineers concrete evidence for comparison before changing kernel or firmware settings.
implementation: Deploy a 60-second Universal Forwarder scripted input that emits one JSON sample for each canonical `/sys/devices/system/cpu/cpufreq/policy*` directory with a readable `stats/total_trans`. Build a seven-day baseline by host, policy, driver, and governor; approve an explicit transition-rate threshold for each monitored policy, then schedule the search over delayed completed five-minute buckets.
visualization: Use a timechart of `transitions_per_minute` with the configured threshold overlaid and split by host/policy, plus a table of driver, governor, affected CPUs, observed seconds, transition count, rate, and latest contextual frequency. Add a data-quality panel showing latest sample time and policies missing threshold rows. Label frequency as MHz only after dividing the source kHz value by 1000, and never label transition rate as thermal-throttle count.

Splunk: Get data through scripted inputs

knownFalsePositives:
The counter deltas are genuine CPUFreq statistics; these are common benign reasons for an above-baseline page rather than reasons to call the event fabricated.

1. **`stress-ng --cpu` performance exercise** — A scheduled benchmark can make `schedutil` or `ondemand` change requested states rapidly. Match the host and interval to the named performance-test ticket and the `stress-ng` process; use an exact, time-bounded row in `linux_cpufreq_exceptions.csv` instead of raising the fleet threshold.

2. **`tuned-adm` profile rollout** — Changing between `powersave`, `balanced`, and `throughput-performance` profiles can alter governor behavior and briefly exceed the old baseline. Confirm `tuned.service` change logs and the approved configuration-management run, then suppress only the affected host/policy during the change window and re-baseline after the profile is stable.

3. **Kernel or CPU microcode maintenance** — A kernel boot, CPUFreq driver reload, or microcode rollout can change policy numbering, available frequencies, driver behavior, or reset `total_trans`. Correlate boot ID, package version, and change record; the SPL already drops decreasing counters, while a bounded exception covers legitimate post-boot adaptation without hiding later churn.

4. **Build-server compilation burst** — A known Jenkins or GitLab runner compiling a large codebase may legitimately oscillate between busy and idle phases. Confirm the runner job ID, process timing, and expected host role; route the finding to capacity telemetry or apply a short exact exception for that job, not a permanent exception for all build hosts.

5. **Latency-sensitive service with an intentionally reactive governor** — A trading gateway or packet-processing worker may have a stable, reviewed transition rate that is abnormal for general servers. Compare the result with that host/policy's seven-day baseline and approved power profile; store a higher reviewed threshold in `linux_cpufreq_thresholds.csv` rather than suppressing every result.

6. **Collector duplication through `cpu*/cpufreq` symlinks** — Polling per-CPU symlinks can emit several copies of one shared policy and make dashboards look busier, even though this SPL groups the canonical `policy` field. Verify the script enumerates only `/sys/devices/system/cpu/cpufreq/policy*`, compare identical `sample_epoch,total_trans` tuples, and fix the collector; do not add an exception for duplicate ingestion.

**Suppression mechanism — time-bound exception:** `linux_cpufreq_exceptions.csv` must contain one unique exact `host,policy` key plus numeric `exception_start_epoch`, `exception_end_epoch`, `exception_enabled`, owner, reason, and `exception_ticket`. Permit only approved, finite windows; retain raw samples and the unsuppressed base report. Baseline tuning belongs in the separately governed `linux_cpufreq_thresholds.csv` lookup.
reviewer: documentation review against Linux kernel CPUFreq, systemd journal, Linux Audit, and Splunk primary sources; no runtime or hardware-SME sign-off
mitreAttack: N/A (operational CPU performance observability; not a security detection)
detailedImplementation:
## Prerequisites and signal semantics

Use a Linux system where `/sys/devices/system/cpu/cpufreq/policy*` exists and at least one policy exposes readable `stats/total_trans`. The policy directory is the canonical unit: several logical CPUs may share one hardware performance-control interface and point to the same policy through `cpu*/cpufreq` symlinks. `CONFIG_CPU_FREQ_STAT` must be available; when `stats/total_trans` is absent, this use case has no supported transition counter and must report a collection-coverage gap rather than infer events from frequency samples.

The kernel documents `total_trans` as a cumulative count since CPUFreq statistics were loaded or reset. It is not a systemd event stream and it may not represent every autonomous hardware P-state adjustment. The kernel reports `scaling_cur_freq` in kHz, but its closeness to instantaneous hardware frequency is architecture-dependent. Consequently, this design computes deltas only from `total_trans`, treats counter decreases as resets, and converts optional kHz context to MHz by dividing by 1000. A high transition rate is not proof of heat, throttling, or power trouble.

Install Splunk Universal Forwarder according to the deployment's supported platform matrix. No Splunkbase add-on is required. The example collector requires a host-managed Python 3 interpreter; verify `/usr/bin/python3` and package ownership rather than assuming that the Forwarder bundles a suitable runtime. Give the Forwarder service account read access only to the exposed sysfs attributes and write access to its own logs. Capacity is approximately one short JSON event per CPUFreq policy per minute: a four-policy host yields about 5,760 events/day before indexing overhead. Confirm index access, scripted-input deployment rights, lookup-edit ownership, and search/alert permissions.

## Step 1 — Configure data collection

Create a deployment app such as `$SPLUNK_HOME/etc/apps/linux_cpufreq`. Place the reviewed code from `scriptExample` in `bin/collect_cpufreq.py` and an executable `bin/collect_cpufreq.sh` wrapper that clears inherited library-path variables and runs `/usr/bin/python3 "$SPLUNK_HOME/etc/apps/linux_cpufreq/bin/collect_cpufreq.py"`. Keep code ownership with the deployment administrator and deny writes by unprivileged users. In `local/inputs.conf`, configure `[script://$SPLUNK_HOME/etc/apps/linux_cpufreq/bin/collect_cpufreq.sh]`, `disabled = 0`, `interval = 60`, `index = os`, and `sourcetype = linux:cpufreq:stats`. `os` and the sourcetype are local conventions and must be changed consistently in the input and SPL if the deployment uses other names.

The collector emits one compact JSON line per canonical policy. Configure parsing for one event per line with `SHOULD_LINEMERGE = false` and `LINE_BREAKER = ([\r\n]+)` for `[linux:cpufreq:stats]`; use `DATETIME_CONFIG = CURRENT` because `sample_epoch` is deliberately applied in SPL and preserves sample time without relying on automatic JSON timestamp recognition. The primary SPL runs `spath`, so indexed JSON field extraction is not required. Do not poll `/sys/devices/system/cpu/cpu*/cpufreq`, which can duplicate shared policies. Do not install an Audit watch on `scaling_cur_freq`: an inode/syscall watch is not a documented feed for kernel-internal value updates. Likewise, journald can carry driver diagnostics but systemd defines no standard record per CPUFreq transition.

Before deployment, run the wrapper as the Forwarder service account. Every stdout line must parse as JSON; stderr is reserved for actionable collector errors and appears in `splunkd.log`. Deploy and inspect the effective stanza with `splunk btool inputs list --debug`. In Splunk, run `index=os sourcetype=linux:cpufreq:stats earliest=-10m | spath | table _time host sample_epoch policy total_trans affected_cpus related_cpus scaling_driver scaling_governor current_frequency_khz`. Compare two successive `total_trans` values with direct reads of the same policy. Missing optional `scaling_cur_freq` is acceptable; missing `total_trans` makes that policy unsupported.

Create `linux_cpufreq_thresholds.csv` with one unique row per exact `host,policy` and numeric `max_transitions_per_minute,min_observed_seconds,threshold_enabled`. Start `min_observed_seconds` at 180 so a five-minute result is not based on one short interval. Create `linux_cpufreq_exceptions.csv` with unique exact keys and the fields named in `knownFalsePositives`. Define both as lookup definitions and restrict write access to the Linux platform owner.

## Step 2 — Create the search and alert

Do not ship a universal transition threshold. Drivers, governors, CPU topology, polling cadence, and workload shape differ enough that the former `count > 10` rule had no defensible unit or meaning. Collect at least seven representative days spanning normal batch and interactive periods. Using the same delta logic as the primary SPL but without either lookup, chart five-minute `transitions_per_minute` by host and policy and split comparisons when `scaling_driver` or `scaling_governor` changes. Review the median, 95th, and 99th percentiles with the service owner. Set `max_transitions_per_minute` above known benign peaks but below the rate associated with the performance condition the team has agreed to investigate; document the measurement window and ticket. A threshold row is intentionally mandatory, so an unreviewed policy cannot silently inherit an arbitrary number.

Save the exact `spl` field as `linux_cpufreq_transition_rate_5m`. `spath` extracts each JSON line and `tonumber` makes units explicit. Replacing `_time` with `sample_epoch` prevents forwarding delay from becoming the rate denominator. After sorting, `streamstats current=f window=1` attaches the immediately preceding counter and time for the same host/policy. The search discards first samples, zero/negative elapsed time, and counter decreases. It timestamps each delta at the midpoint of its interval, rolls deltas into five-minute buckets, and computes `transitions_per_minute = transition_count * 60 / observed_seconds`. The threshold lookup requires both sufficient coverage and an enabled reviewed limit. The exception lookup suppresses only an exact active host/policy window.

Schedule at five-minute intervals with a measured ingestion delay. For a one-minute poll and approximately two minutes of indexing allowance, a minute-offset cron such as `2-57/5 * * * *` can search `earliest=-8m@m latest=-2m@m`: this includes one predecessor sample and one completed five-minute bucket. Measure `_indextime-sample_epoch` before accepting those bounds; increase the delay if late data is normal and avoid overlapping alert windows. Trigger when result count is greater than zero, throttle by `host,policy` for 30 minutes, and attach the threshold, driver, governor, rate, observed seconds, and a raw-event drilldown. Keep a separate unsuppressed report for audit and tuning. There is no CIM data-model alternative for these custom kernel policy counters.

## Step 3 — Validate counters, units, and controls

Run the positive and negative fixtures in `controlTest` against a nonproduction index and test lookup definitions. The five increasing counters must yield 240 transitions over 240 seconds, or 60 transitions/minute, and cross the fixture's 30 transitions/minute threshold. Alternating `scaling_cur_freq` with a flat counter must not alert. A reset must lose only the reset interval; it must not create a wrapped or negative rate. Activate the exact exception and verify that the alert result disappears while the raw events and a version of the search before the final exception filter still show the sequence.

On an approved test host, record two direct reads at least one poll apart from `/sys/devices/system/cpu/cpufreq/policy0/stats/total_trans`; compare their difference and elapsed wall time with the corresponding Splunk row. Confirm that `current_frequency_khz=2400000` renders as `current_frequency_mhz=2400`, not 2,400,000 MHz or 2.4 MHz. Compare the policy's `affected_cpus`, `scaling_driver`, and `scaling_governor` with sysfs. Run a 24-hour `timechart span=1m count by policy` and flag missing polls, duplicate events, and policy cardinality changes. Documentation review does not claim that these runtime tests were performed in a production or customer environment.

## Step 4 — Operationalize and respond

Build the dashboard described in `visualization` with a 24-hour operational picker and seven-day baseline view. Add a single-value panel for monitored policies versus policies missing an enabled threshold, because silence caused by absent lookup rows is configuration state, not healthy performance. Limit raw-event and lookup editing to Linux platform engineers; consumers may view rates and approved threshold metadata.

When a result fires, first establish whether the host, policy, driver, governor, and affected CPU set are expected. Correlate the interval with workload latency, CPU utilization, scheduler pressure, deployment, kernel boot, `tuned` activity, and firmware or microcode changes. Compare current and baseline transition rates using the same driver/governor cohort. If user impact and a configuration change coincide, follow the approved rollback process; do not change governors, min/max frequencies, BIOS settings, or thermal controls directly from this alert. Escalate persistent unexplained churn with raw samples, kernel and microcode versions, policy attributes, workload evidence, and the threshold rationale. Use dedicated thermal-zone, cooling-device, or hardware telemetry before describing the incident as thermal throttling.

## Step 5 — Troubleshoot and govern exceptions

No policy events usually means CPUFreq is unavailable, firmware controls frequency without a Linux policy, the guest exposes no interface, `CONFIG_CPU_FREQ_STAT` is disabled, or the service account cannot read `stats/total_trans`. Confirm the canonical policy path before changing permissions. Events with only metadata but no `total_trans` indicate the script was modified to emit unsupported records; restore the skip behavior. Errors in `splunkd.log` mentioning Python or shared libraries indicate a missing host runtime, an inherited `LD_LIBRARY_PATH`, a non-executable wrapper, or package path drift; test the wrapper in the Forwarder environment.

Duplicate samples with identical `sample_epoch,policy,total_trans` usually mean overlapping deployment apps or per-CPU symlink enumeration. Find the effective stanzas with `btool` and retain one canonical input. Rates of zero despite visible `scaling_cur_freq` variation are not necessarily wrong: the sampled value and cpufreq-stats transition accounting have different semantics and driver/hardware behavior matters. Missing results with healthy raw data usually mean there is no unique enabled threshold, `min_observed_seconds` is too high for actual coverage, the scheduled window lacks a predecessor sample, or an exception is active. Inspect lookup matches before loosening the SPL. Gaps after reboot may reflect policy renumbering or delayed driver initialization; require a newly reviewed threshold for a new key rather than silently copying one.

Review thresholds after kernel, firmware, governor, CPU topology, or major workload changes and at least quarterly. Every exception needs a finite start and end, owner, reason, and ticket. Reject wildcard hosts, wildcard policies, and indefinite end times. Expired rows should be disabled or removed during the review, while raw samples and unsuppressed reports remain available for trend analysis.
grandmaExplanation: We count how often a Linux computer changes its processor speed and compare that pace with what is normal for that specific machine. An unusual burst helps the operations team investigate a performance or power-setting change without pretending it automatically means the computer is overheating.
